content: 1. A randomized controlled trial conducted in 2015 evaluated the use of osmotic dilators alone for cervical preparation prior to dilation and evacuation. The study was published in Obstetrics and Gynecology. 2. Another randomized controlled trial in 2014 investigated the combination of buccal misoprostol and laminaria for cervical preparation before dilation and evacuation at 21–23 weeks of gestation. This study was published in Contraception. 3. A 2016 randomized controlled trial assessed the use of synthetic osmotic dilators with adjunctive misoprostol for same-day dilation and evacuation. The findings were also published in Contraception. 4. Client satisfaction with the intervention was moderate, with 768 per 1,000 clients reporting satisfaction compared to 686 per 1,000 in the control group. The evidence certainty was rated as moderate. 5. Provider satisfaction was not pooled due to the lack of sufficient studies. 6. Side effects such as nausea were significantly reduced in the intervention group, with 58 per 1,000 experiencing nausea compared to 343 per 1,000 in the control group. The evidence certainty was high. 7. Vomiting was also less frequent in the intervention group, with 89 per 1,000 affected compared to 371 per 1,000 in the control group. The evidence certainty was high. 8. Diarrhea rates were similar between groups, with 29 per 1,000 in both the intervention and control groups. The evidence certainty was low. 9. Bleeding outcomes were not pooled due to heterogeneity in the studies. The evidence certainty was low. 10. Cervical tears were not pooled due to insufficient data, and the evidence certainty was very low. 11. Pre-procedure expulsion rates were not pooled due to a lack of studies. 12. The need for additional interventions was not pooled, and the evidence certainty was very low. 13. Uterine perforation rates were not pooled due to a lack of studies. 14. Preand post-procedure pain was assessed in binary outcomes. For a 2-day versus 1-day protocol, 287 per 1,000 experienced pain in the intervention group compared to 219 per 1,000 in the control group. The evidence certainty was low. 15. When comparing synthetic dilators to laminaria, 59 per 1,000 experienced pain in the intervention group compared to 657 per 1,000 in the control group. The evidence certainty was high. 16. Continuous pain outcomes were not pooled due to a lack of studies. 17. Comparative cost and cost to the patient were not pooled due to insufficient data. 18. The combination of letrozole and misoprostol was found to be a safe and effective option for medical abortion. Letrozole was administered orally at 10 mg daily for 3 days, followed by 800 μg of misoprostol sublingually on the fourth day. 19. Fewer women in the letrozole plus misoprostol group had ongoing pregnancies compared to the misoprostol-alone group. The evidence certainty was low. 20. Successful abortion rates (uterine emptying without surgical intervention) were higher in the letrozole plus misoprostol group compared to the misoprostol-alone group. The evidence certainty was very low. 21. Expulsion time was shorter in the letrozole plus misoprostol group compared to the misoprostol-alone group. 22. Fewer women in the letrozole plus misoprostol group experienced lower abdominal pain compared to the misoprostol-alone group. The evidence certainty was moderate. 23. Nausea and vomiting were less frequent in the letrozole plus misoprostol group compared to the misoprostol-alone group. The evidence certainty was moderate for nausea and low for vomiting. 24. Diarrhea was less frequent in the letrozole plus misoprostol group compared to the misoprostol-alone group. The evidence certainty was low. 25. Fever and chills/rigors were more frequent in the letrozole plus misoprostol group compared to the misoprostol-alone group. The evidence certainty was high. 26. The combination of mifepristone and misoprostol is recommended over misoprostol alone for medical management of missed abortion at less than 14 weeks of gestation. The recommended regimen includes 200 mg of mifepristone orally, followed by 800 μg of misoprostol administered buccally, sublingually, or vaginally. 27. Medical management with mifepristone plus misoprostol was found to be a safe, effective, and satisfactory alternative to misoprostol alone for missed abortion at less than 14 weeks of gestation. 28. Medical management (all regimens) was found to be a safe, effective, and satisfactory alternative to expectant management for missed abortion at less than 14 weeks of gestation. 29. Surgical management was found to be a safe, effective, and satisfactory alternative to medical or expectant management for missed abortion at less than 14 weeks of gestation. 30. A systematic review identified 20 studies on the management of missed abortion, with 19 studies comparing mifepristone plus misoprostol versus misoprostol alone, medical versus expectant management, and surgical versus medical/expectant management. The studies were conducted in various global settings, including China, India, Sweden, and the USA.
